1 📚 What a hash table is
├── 1.1 A hash table is a data structure that stores key-value pairs and finds any entry in roughly constant time.
├── 1.2 A hash function turns each key into an array index, so a lookup jumps straight to the right slot instead of scanning.
└── 1.3 Different keys can hash to the same slot, so collisions are resolved by chaining entries in a list or probing for another open slot.

message.content: In three sentences, explain what a binary search tree is.

content.text:
Response (👀 no changes made)

1 🌳 What a binary search tree is
├── 1.1 A binary search tree is a data structure where each node holds a key and has at most two children.
├── 1.2 Every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key and every key in its right subtree is larger, so a search discards half the remaining nodes at each step.
└── 1.3 That ordering gives logarithmic search, insert, and delete on a balanced tree, but degrades to linear time when insertions arrive in sorted order and the tree becomes a chain.

content.text:
Response (👀 no changes made)

1 🔗 What a linked list is
├── 1.1 A linked list is a data structure where each element sits in its own node holding a value and a pointer to the next node.
├── 1.2 The nodes are not stored contiguously, so reaching the nth element means walking the chain from the head rather than indexing directly.
└── 1.3 That layout makes inserting or removing at a known position cheap, since only a couple of pointers change instead of shifting every later element.

content.text:
Response (👀 no changes made)

1 🚶 What a queue is
├── 1.1 A queue is a data structure that serves elements in first-in-first-out order, like a line at a counter.
├── 1.2 The two core operations are enqueue, which adds an element at the back, and dequeue, which removes the element at the front.
└── 1.3 Backing it with a linked list or a circular array keeps both operations constant time, which is why queues underpin task schedulers, message buffers, and breadth-first search.

1 📚 What a stack is
├── 1.1 A stack is a data structure that serves elements in last-in-first-out order, like a pile of plates.
├── 1.2 The two core operations are push, which adds an element on top, and pop, which removes the most recently added one.
└── 1.3 Both run in constant time over an array or linked list, which is why stacks back call frames, undo history, expression evaluation, and depth-first search.

1 🕸️ What a graph is
├── 1.1 A graph is a data structure made of vertices and the edges connecting them, modeling arbitrary relationships rather than a single linear or hierarchical order.
├── 1.2 Edges may be directed or undirected and carry weights, which is how graphs express one-way links, mutual connections, and costs like distance.
└── 1.3 The usual representations are an adjacency list, which is compact for sparse graphs, and an adjacency matrix, which makes edge lookup constant time at the cost of space.
